lead: Dividing up work isn't just about who's faster; it's also about what each person gives up to do it.
when: When a team or household needs to divide up work and one person seems faster at everything, or you want to understand why people with different abilities can still help each other.
body:
A coworker is fast at making reports and fast at making posters. Should you hand him both kinds of tasks? Not necessarily. Besides who's faster, you need to look at how much of the other kind of output he gives up by spending his time on one, and how the team can best be combined.

Comparative advantage is the relative advantage a person or organization has in carrying out an activity at a lower opportunity cost; it differs from absolute advantage, which means doing it faster or with fewer resources.

Comparative advantage uses opportunity cost to compare ways of dividing work. Even if someone is slower at both tasks, they may give up relatively less on one of them, which makes them a good partner for it. That word "relative" matters. It's not simply about finding the job each person likes most or feels most confident in.

Real teams also have to consider quality, learning, handoffs, deadlines, and fairness, so you can't lock everyone into roles based on a single timesheet. Comparative advantage offers one angle of analysis. It doesn't mean everyone should only ever do what they're best at right now.

In the matrix, rows are people and columns are tasks, with quality and units kept consistent first. Raw times only show who's faster in absolute terms; comparative advantage also compares the same person's two tasks to work out how much of the other output is given up.
example:
Here are some made-up times. Alex takes 1 hour for a report and 3 hours for a poster; Sam takes 4 hours for a report and 5 hours for a poster. Alex is faster at both, but a report costs Alex only one-third of a poster, while it costs Sam four-fifths of a poster. So Alex has the comparative advantage in reports. Flip it around, and Sam has the lower opportunity cost for posters.

If you need two reports and two posters, having each person do one of each takes 13 hours of work in total; having Alex do both reports and Sam do both posters takes 12. This is only a simplified comparison of total work hours. When things actually get finished also depends on whether work can happen in parallel, handoffs, and quality, so "fewer work hours" doesn't automatically mean "delivered sooner."
extra:
Two roommates splitting chores shouldn't just say, "You're better at everything than me, so you do it all." They can compare how much time and effort each of them spends on cooking, tidying, and shopping, then talk about how to divide and trade.

Even if one arrangement saves more time, both people should have a say, a chance to practice, and reasonable rest. If the efficiency gains only benefit one person, the arrangement may not last.
steps: With quality kept roughly equal, list the resources and time each person needs for each task.
Compare how much other output is given up for each task, separating relative opportunity cost from absolute speed.
Bring handoffs, deadlines, fairness, and learning needs into the discussion, then try the division of work and review it.
caution: This depends on tasks, resources, and opportunity costs that can be compared, so you can't apply fixed ratios to every kind of work. Professional quality, coordination costs, learning over time, and power differences can all change the arrangement. Comparative advantage isn't an inborn identity either, and it should never be used to justify making someone carry work they don't want to do over the long term.
exercise: Pick two people and two comparable tasks, and write down rough times and quality requirements. First see who's faster, then separately work out how much of one task is given up to do the other, and see whether the conclusions match.
brief: Two stick figures face two kinds of tasks, organizing documents and graphic design; they first compare hourglasses of different shapes, then each focus on one kind and swap their results. Neither is drawn as incompetent.
diagramCaption: The top row is Alex and the bottom row is Sam; the left column is reports and the right column is posters, with each small block standing for 1 hour. Absolute times are compared down the same column, while opportunity cost is worked out along the same row. All data is hypothetical.
